strengths: Addresses a meaningful problem: training deep SNNs with separate excitatory and inhibitory populations without batch normalization.
Demonstrates successful training of VGG-16/19 and ResNet-18 at four time steps, reaching 92.12% on CIFAR-10 and 65.53% on CIFAR-100 and outperforming the reported E-I-constrained baselines.
Provides an interpretable initialization scheme with explicit moment calculations, stabilization pseudocode, and useful evidence that inhibitory-gradient scaling affects training stability.
weaknesses: Comparisons do not convincingly isolate the contribution. Most competing methods use different architectures, time steps, and potentially training recipes; parameter counts and computational costs are absent. The matched CIFAR-10 BN baselines outperform the proposed models by 2.98–3.62 percentage points, and no corresponding CIFAR-100 BN baseline is reported.

Evaluation is limited to two closely related static-image datasets, with no repeated-run statistics, temporal tasks, or larger-scale benchmarks. This provides insufficient support for broad claims about scalability, robustness, and temporal cortical computation.

The ablations do not establish that every component is indispensable. There is no isolated STE ablation, no separate removal of subtractive versus divisive inhibition, and no comparison with Cornford-style initialization within the same SNN. Fixed-epsilon alternatives are tested only from 1e-8 to 1e-5. Clamped Kaiming initialization still achieves 85.61% versus 87.03%, contradicting an unqualified necessity claim.

The stabilization rule addresses exactly zero denominators, although the stated problem includes near-zero values. Arbitrarily small positive denominators remain unchanged, and Algorithm 1 produces infinity when an entire sample is zero. These cases need explicit treatment and stability evidence.

Biological-realism claims exceed the demonstrated properties. Inhibitory neurons are implemented as instantaneous real-valued ReLUs, and stabilization requires a minimum across each sample. The derivation of spike count from the fast-LIF limit is not justified by the time-constant argument alone. These approximations need validation before positioning the model as a platform for cortical dynamics.

Important implementation details are missing: enforcement of nonnegative weights during optimization, constraints on trainable gains, the excitatory spike surrogate, convolutional E-I connectivity, and handling of signed direct-encoded inputs during Bernoulli-based initialization. Code is promised only upon publication, limiting verification of Dale compliance and reproducibility.

Novelty relative to Cornford et al.'s E-I architecture and initialization is insufficiently isolated. The remaining additions largely combine moment matching, an STE, denominator replacement, and gradient scaling; stronger controlled evidence is needed to establish their significance. Likewise, current histograms and one feature-map example do not establish the claimed functional distinction from normalization or general emergence of sparse, edge-focused representations.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: training deep SNNs with separate excitatory and inhibitory populations without batch normalization. Combining activity balancing, divisive inhibition, and gradient stabilization provides a coherent engineering framework.

The reported results demonstrate feasible training of VGG-16/19 and ResNet-18 with four time steps, reaching 92.12% on CIFAR-10 and 65.53% on CIFAR-100. Comparisons with DANN across several depths provide useful evidence beyond a single architecture.

The manuscript includes initialization derivations, stabilization pseudocode, training hyperparameters, and diagnostic visualizations. The ablations identify concrete training failures associated with some alternative configurations.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not convincingly isolate the contribution. Most normalization-free and E-I SNN comparisons in Table 1 use different architectures and time budgets, without matched parameter counts or training protocols. The matched CIFAR-10 BN baselines outperform the proposed models by 2.98–3.62 percentage points; CIFAR-100 lacks a corresponding BN comparison. These results establish feasibility more clearly than competitive performance.

The novelty relative to Cornford et al. is insufficiently established. The initialization explicitly builds on that work, while STE and gradient scaling are established techniques. Comparing final accuracy against a rate-based DANN does not isolate the benefit of the proposed initialization and propagation rules from differences in neuronal dynamics. A direct adaptation of the prior E-I approach to the same SNN backbone would be a more informative baseline.

The ablations do not support the claim that every component is indispensable. Clamped Kaiming initialization on WEE and WIE still achieves 85.61%, versus 87.03% for the full method. There is no isolated STE ablation, no separation of subtractive and divisive inhibition, and no comparison against the prior E-I initialization. The epsilon sweep covers only 10^-8 to 10^-5 and does not rule out appropriately tuned denominator floors. All ablations use VGG-8, leaving their relevance to the deeper headline models uncertain.

The adaptive stabilization rule has unresolved technical limitations. Replacing exact zeros with the smallest positive entry does not protect against arbitrarily small positive denominators, despite near-zero values being the stated problem. Algorithm 1 also produces an infinite replacement when an entire sample is zero, without explaining the intended behavior. No denominator statistics or multi-seed robustness results establish that these cases are adequately handled.

The biological-realism claims exceed the evidence. Inhibitory neurons are implemented as instantaneous real-valued ReLUs, and the derivation from a fast-spiking LIF neuron to the spike-count approximation in Equation 7 is not validated. Sample-wide minimum replacement and backpropagation are computational devices without demonstrated biological counterparts. Moreover, the paper does not specify how nonnegative synaptic weights and appropriate gain signs are maintained during optimization, leaving the claimed Dale-law compliance incompletely documented.

The initialization analysis establishes moments under independent Bernoulli inputs and random weights, but does not establish stable propagation through the complete subtractive-divisive LIF circuit. In particular, matching the expected denominator to the standard deviation of the excitatory current does not determine the variance of their correlated ratio. The first layer receives signed, normalized image values rather than Bernoulli spikes, yet its initialization treatment is not explained.

Experimental scope and reproducibility remain limited: only two related static-image datasets are evaluated, with no temporal task, repeated-run uncertainty, or computational-overhead measurements. Important implementation details—including convolutional inhibitory connectivity, spike surrogate gradients, sign enforcement, and the layerwise initialization procedure—are missing, while code is deferred until publication. Finally, current histograms and one feature-map example do not establish the claimed sparse, edge-selective computational mechanism or its functional distinction from normalization.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful problem: training deep SNNs with separate excitatory and inhibitory populations without conventional normalization layers.

Demonstrates successful training across several VGG depths, ResNet-18, and five static/event-based datasets. The reproduced DANN comparisons provide useful evidence of improved accuracy under E-I constraints.
Provides initialization derivations, implementation pseudocode, component ablations, gradient-scaling sensitivity results, and transparent computational-overhead measurements.
weaknesses: The biological justification contains a substantive mathematical error. Appendix D.1 derives subthreshold relaxation but then identifies spike count with floor(ReLU(I0)), ignoring repeated threshold crossings and resets. For a constant suprathreshold current, the stated LIF model instead has interspike interval τI log(I0/(I0−θI)); its spike count depends on Δt/τI. Thus, fast relaxation alone does not justify the claimed rigorous ReLU approximation.

The central stability mechanism is incompletely justified. Algorithm 2 replaces exact zeros but leaves arbitrarily small positive denominators unchanged, despite near-zero denominators motivating the method. An entirely zero sample produces an infinite replacement value. These cases need explicit treatment and empirical diagnostics.

Ablations do not establish that every component is indispensable. Clamped Kaiming initialization still achieves 85.61% versus 87.03%, STE is not independently ablated, and subtractive/divisive inhibition are not isolated. Testing fixed epsilon only from 10−8 to 10−5 does not exclude appropriately scaled denominator floors or other standard stabilization methods.

Comparative evidence is insufficient for broad competitiveness claims. CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 trails the reproduced BN baseline by 3.32 percentage points, and CIFAR-100 trails listed normalization methods substantially. Most normalization-free comparisons use different architectures and training protocols; TinyImageNet has no baseline, and DVS-Gesture has only one. Matched comparisons with strong normalization-free and E-I-constrained SNNs are needed.

Novelty over Cornford et al. is insufficiently isolated. The paper explicitly builds on its E-I initialization, while the additional ingredients are data-dependent scaling, denominator replacement, STE, and gradient scaling. Comparisons against direct adaptations of the prior initialization to the same SNN would better establish the specific methodological advance.

Important reproduction details are missing: the excitatory spike surrogate derivative, enforcement of nonnegative weights throughout optimization, and constraints on trainable gains. These affect both trainability and the claimed E-I semantics. Code is deferred until publication, and the run count underlying the proposed method’s error bars is not clearly specified.

Biological and functional conclusions exceed the evidence. Initialization explicitly uses batch statistics, stabilization requires a sample-wide minimum, and inhibitory units are continuous stateless units. Moreover, BN does not generally make distributions Gaussian, so the histogram comparison does not establish a fundamentally distinct computational mechanism. No physiological validation supports the broader cortical-modeling claims.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful problem: training deep SNNs with separate excitatory and inhibitory populations without conventional normalization layers.
Demonstrates working models across five static and event-based datasets, including VGG-19 and ResNet-18. Results are promising relative to several reported normalization-free baselines.
Includes reproduced BN and DANN comparisons, component ablations, gradient-scaling sensitivity experiments, implementation pseudocode, and transparent computational-overhead measurements.
weaknesses: The biological justification contains a substantive mathematical gap. Appendix D.1 derives the subthreshold equilibrium of a LIF neuron, then asserts that its spike count is approximately ReLU(input). This does not follow when threshold crossings and resets are included: spike counts depend on the time constant and observation interval. The claimed rigorous fast-spiking approximation therefore does not establish the validity of the continuous inhibitory units.

The stabilization mechanism only replaces exactly zero denominators; it does not bound arbitrarily small positive denominators, despite near-zero values being the stated source of instability. Algorithm 2 also lacks a meaningful finite fallback when an entire sample has zero inhibitory activity. Consequently, its general stability claims exceed the evidence.

Ablations do not establish that every proposed component is indispensable. Clamped Kaiming initialization still achieves 85.61% versus 87.03% for the full method. There is no isolated STE ablation or separate evaluation of subtractive and divisive inhibition, and the fixed-epsilon comparison tests only 1e-8 through 1e-5 without broader tuning or alternative stabilization strategies.

Comparative evidence is insufficient for the broad competitiveness and scalability claims. On matched CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 models, accuracy falls from 95.37% with BN to 92.05%. Most normalization-free comparisons use different architectures and training protocols; TinyImageNet has no baseline and is downsampled to 32×32. Training also costs approximately 2.3–2.5 times as much as the BN baseline.

The conceptual advance over prior E-I networks needs clearer isolation. The framework combines an acknowledged prior initialization approach with moment matching, continuous inhibitory units, an STE, and gradient rescaling. DANN comparisons change both neuronal dynamics and training mechanisms, leaving the source of improvement unresolved.

Biological and functional conclusions are overstated. Initialization uses batch statistics, stabilization requires a sample-wide minimum, and inhibitory units are continuous rather than explicitly simulated spiking neurons. Moreover, BN does not inherently Gaussianize distributions, so the bimodal histograms in Section 5.3 do not establish a fundamentally distinct regulatory mechanism or identify stable activated and suppressed populations.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified, including the excitatory spike surrogate gradient and how weight signs and gain positivity are maintained during optimization. These directly affect trainability and the claimed E-I constraints. Code is promised only upon publication.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: training deep SNNs with separate excitatory and inhibitory populations without conventional normalization layers. The integration of initialization, divisive inhibition, and gradient stabilization provides a concrete working framework.

Experiments cover five static and event-based datasets and multiple VGG and ResNet architectures. Results demonstrate feasible training under E–I constraints, including 92.05% on CIFAR-10 with four time steps and 77.66% on CIFAR10-DVS.

Reproduced DANN comparisons provide useful evidence of improvement over an existing E–I-constrained ANN approach. Ablations and gradient-scale sensitivity experiments help identify important stabilization mechanisms.
The appendices provide initialization and stabilization pseudocode, training configurations, and transparent measurements of training-time and memory overhead.
weaknesses: The claimed rigorous derivation of inhibitory activity is incorrect (Section 3.2 and Appendix D.1). Convergence of the subthreshold voltage to the input current does not imply that the spike count equals the floor of that current. With threshold 1, reset to 0, and constant current I > 1, the LIF interspike interval is τI log(I/(I−1)); the count therefore depends on τI and the observation interval. For 0 < I < 1, the neuron does not fire, whereas the proposed ReLU approximation is positive. A stateless rate model may be a useful design choice, but the stated proof does not establish it, weakening the central biological justification.

The evaluation does not convincingly establish competitiveness under controlled conditions. Most comparisons change architecture, time steps, or training protocol, and parameter-matched comparisons are absent despite the additional inhibitory pathways. The reproduced CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 BN baseline reaches 95.37%, versus 92.05% for the proposal; CIFAR-100 results also substantially trail listed normalization-based methods. TinyImageNet has no comparison baseline and is downsampled to 32×32, making the scalability claim difficult to assess.

The ablations do not support the claim that every component is indispensable. Clamped Kaiming initialization still trains to 85.61%, versus 87.03% with E-I Init. There is no isolated STE ablation, no separation of subtractive and divisive inhibition, and no comparison against adapting the cited DANN initialization to the same SNN. Testing fixed epsilon only from 10^-8 to 10^-5 does not establish that adaptive replacement is necessary.

The stabilization mechanism has unresolved edge cases and limited guarantees (Algorithm 2). It replaces exact zeros but leaves arbitrarily small positive denominators unchanged. For an entirely zero sample, its minimum becomes infinity rather than a finite stabilizer. The method also requires a sample-wide minimum, while initialization explicitly uses batch statistics; the biological implementation of these operations is not addressed.

Biological and functional claims exceed the evidence. Inhibitory units are continuous, stateless units, and training uses backpropagation plus engineered gradient scaling. No validation against explicit fast-spiking inhibitory dynamics or biological measurements is provided. Moreover, BN does not generally enforce Gaussian output distributions, so the bimodal histograms in Section 5.3 do not establish the claimed mechanistic distinction or functional benefit.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified, including the spike surrogate derivative and how nonnegative weights and appropriate gain constraints are maintained during optimization. Event binning and the CIFAR10-DVS split are insufficiently described. Code is promised only after publication, and reporting the best validation accuracy across epochs without a separate selection protocol limits confidence in small improvements.

Practical benefits remain uncertain: measured training time increases by approximately 2.3–2.5× and memory by up to 1.57×. No inference-energy or hardware measurements establish an offsetting deployment advantage. Together with the derivation and evaluation issues, this leaves the contribution below the acceptance threshold despite its promising empirical feasibility.
